```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "##", fig.align = "center")
```

# Install NNS

We need the latest version of NNS available on GitHub.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
require(devtools); install_github('OVVO-Financial/NNS', ref = "NNS-Beta-Version")
```

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
require(NNS)
require(data.table)
```

# Data

Let's create a spiral dataset.

```{r data, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 5}
N <- 200 # number of points per class
D <- 2 # dimensionality
K <- 4 # number of classes
X <- data.frame() # data matrix (each row = single example)
y <- data.frame() # class labels
set.seed(123)
for (j in (1:K)) {
  r <- seq(0.05, 1, length.out = N) # radius
  t <- seq((j - 1) * 4.7, j * 4.7, length.out = N) # theta
  Xtemp <- data.frame(x = r * sin(t), y = r * cos(t))
  ytemp <- data.frame(matrix(j, N, 1))
  X <- rbind(X, Xtemp)
  y <- rbind(y, ytemp)
}
data <- cbind(X, y)
colnames(data) <- c(colnames(X), 'label')
plot(data[, 1], data[, 2], col = 'steelblue', xlab = 'x', ylab = 'y')
```

# More Data

Next we will create two more spirals. The second spiral will have a noise term
added to the first spiral. The third spiral will have a different seed and the
same noise term added.

```{r more-data}
X <- data.frame() # data matrix (each row = single example)
y <- data.frame() # class labels
set.seed(123)
for (j in (1:K)) {
  r <- seq(0.05, 1, length.out = N) # radius
  t <- seq((j - 1) * 4.7, j * 4.7, length.out = N) + rnorm(N, sd = 0.1) # theta
  Xtemp <- data.frame(x = r * sin(t), y = r * cos(t))
  ytemp <- data.frame(matrix(j, N, 1))
  X <- rbind(X, Xtemp)
  y <- rbind(y, ytemp)
}
data2 <- cbind(X, y)
colnames(data2) <- c(colnames(X), 'label')

X <- data.frame() # data matrix (each row = single example)
y <- data.frame() # class labels
set.seed(1234)
for (j in (1:K)) {
  r <- seq(0.05, 1, length.out = N) # radius
  t <- seq((j - 1) * 4.7, j * 4.7, length.out = N) + rnorm(N, sd = 0.1) # theta
  Xtemp <- data.frame(x = r * sin(t), y = r * cos(t))
  ytemp <- data.frame(matrix(j, N, 1))
  X <- rbind(X, Xtemp)
  y <- rbind(y, ytemp)
}
data3 <- cbind(X, y)
colnames(data3) <- c(colnames(X), 'label')
```

# Simple Correlation Analysis

Does a simple correlation distinguish these spirals from one another? No,
unfortunately all of the x's are correlated and all of the y's are correlated.

```{r pearson}
options(digits = 4)
cor(cbind(data$x, data2$x, data3$x, data$y, data2$y, data3$y))
```

How about nonlinear NNS correlation?

```{r nns-correlation}
NNS.dep(cbind(data$x, data2$x, data3$x, data$y, data2$y, data3$y))$Correlation
```

Nope, still correlated. We need a different feature to distinguish these
spirals.

# NNS Clustering

Next let's compare all 3 different spirals using the partition map in NNS.
Visually, this is not too different from an analyst placing dots on
fingerprints at feature locations.

```{r partitions, fig.height = 3.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
order = 3
z = as.data.table(NNS.part(data$x, data$y, Voronoi = TRUE, order = order)$regression.points)
z2 = as.data.table(NNS.part(data2$x, data2$y, Voronoi = TRUE, order = order)$regression.points)
z3 = as.data.table(NNS.part(data3$x, data3$y, Voronoi = TRUE, order = order)$regression.points)
```

# Distances

Now we can compare the regression points of each spiral to ascertain whether
they have the same structure. Euclidean distances are used to reduce the
$(x, y)$ coordinates to a single distance metric.

$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2} \qquad (1)$$

## Central Coordinates

Our first step requires a central point for each set of coordinates.
Transforming our equation to:

$$d = \sqrt{(x - \bar{x})^2 + (y - \bar{y})^2} \qquad (2)$$

We subtract our column means from each point, transforming our data tables:

```{r centre}
for (j in c("x", "y")) set(z, j = j, value = z[[j]] - mean(z[[j]]))
for (j in c("x", "y")) set(z2, j = j, value = z2[[j]] - mean(z2[[j]]))
for (j in c("x", "y")) set(z3, j = j, value = z3[[j]] - mean(z3[[j]]))
```

## Squared Distances from Central Coordinates

Borrowing from Pythagoras, we then square the distances from the central
coordinates of each set, sum them, and take their square root.

```{r distances}
z[, Dist := sqrt(sum(x^2, y^2)), by = quadrant]
z2[, Dist := sqrt(sum(x^2, y^2)), by = quadrant]
z3[, Dist := sqrt(sum(x^2, y^2)), by = quadrant]
```

## Hypotenuse

Following our (and Euclid's) Pythagorean guideline, we take the square root of
the summed squares for the hypotenuse, or distance from the central point.

```{r hypotenuse}
dis.1 = z[, Dist]
dis.2 = z2[, Dist]
dis.3 = z3[, Dist]
```

# Comparison

Identical geometric structures (the constellation of NNS points) will have
perfectly correlated distances. But, if the images and constellations are
rotated, how do we reconcile the alignment? Sorting the distances should still
yield identical structures...

Pearson Correlation:

```{r compare-pearson}
cor(cbind(sort(dis.1), sort(dis.2), sort(dis.3)))
```

NNS Correlation:

```{r compare-nns}
NNS.dep(cbind(sort(dis.1), sort(dis.2), sort(dis.3)))$Correlation
```

The 2017 version printed NNS correlations of 0.875 between spirals 1 and 2
and 0.625 and 0.750 against spiral 3, against Pearson correlations of
0.998, 0.999 and 0.997, and concluded that the same-seed spirals 1 and 2 match
while spiral 3 does not. The current `NNS.dep` returns 1 for every pair: each
sorted distance vector is increasing, and NNS correlation is 1 for any
monotone increasing relationship, so this comparison no longer separates
spiral 3.

> **Note (2026).** Matching, association and forecasting are separate tasks.
> A claimed matching accuracy needs an explicit labelled correspondence and a
> held-out evaluation (see `examples/example-corrections.md`).
